doc.title: Paquito D'Rivera — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Jazz as a roach, and jazz born from nothing
summary: Jenkins quotes Jackie McLean that jazz cannot be killed; Paquito says jazz was made from scarce means, like the banjo and drum set.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You know what your fellow NEA Jazz Master, Jackie McLean used to say about that?
He used to say, “Jazz is like the roach; you can’t kill it.” [Both laugh]
No shit; he say that. [Both laugh]

Like the roach; you can’t kill it; very good. Oh, you say it so well, it’s a type of music that’s done in a very creative way. It provides something. Inventing the music—the other thing that my wife always say, “The good cook is the one who cook with what he have.” Anyone can cook with a bowl of ingredients; you have garlic, you have oil, and a chicken wing, well you have to cook with that. And if it tastes good, then you are a good cook, but if you have all the elements in your hand; it’s very easy to be a good cook. And Jazz, it started with nothing. Slaves, people that have a piece of wood, and I don’t know what else, they created a banjo; isn’t that a great invention? The banjo is a drum with four strings.
You need people to play percussion instrument; they create an instrument that, one single man can play all those drums. You see, you call that economy. [Both laugh]
